articles.title: Jennifer Lawrence wanted to talk about her hair. The internet had other ideas.
articles.summary: The reaction to Lawrence's new beauty launch has been less about hair and more about cosmetic surgery speculation. Many say that's unfair.
articles.body:
Jennifer Lawrence launched a hair care brand, but the only thing anyone wants to talk about is her face.

The Academy Award-winning actor began a press tour last week to boost her new low-fuss line, named Mes, and made the rounds. She appeared on the cover of the Cut, showing off said effortless hair. She did Alex Cooper's Call Her Daddy podcast and numerous Q&As with beauty publications. She opened up about motherhood, her breast lift and her anxiety over trying something completely new in launching her brand.

"For the last three years, I have been in this kind of delusional bubble where I can't let doubt in," she told the Cut . "Now I'm experiencing doubt."

But the reaction to her announcement seems to be a collective shrug. Celebrity beauty brands have become nearly ubiquitous, and not everyone can translate their personal brand from the screen to the store. For every huge success like Hailey Bieber's Rhode, there are failures like Scarlett Johansson's recently shuttered the Outset , and fans raised an eyebrow at the idea that Lawrence is known for her hair. (Others questioned her brand's name , pronounced "mess," pointing out similarities to Drybar founder Alli Webb's Messy hair care brand.)

To some, it all felt a bit random; to others, more like a recession indicator. But many felt they didn't need to test the products to find out why the star was making this move.

"I'm good with established haircare and skincare brands with a proven track record," wrote one person on Reddit . "You may be good at singing and acting, but that does not mean I have to buy your brand."

They'd rather talk about Lawrence's appearance. On social media sites like TikTok and Reddit, they called the 36-year-old mother of two "unrecognizable," with many commenters saying they had no idea who she was when they first saw her latest photos.

"She was so beautiful. She doesn't look like herself at all anymore," wrote one person on Reddit . "I keep seeing more and more photos of her recently and had no idea at all it was her until I scrolled enough to see someone say it was her! Mind blown."

Many began to assume that Lawrence had undergone at least an upper blepharoplasty , maybe a facelift and, most likely, both. Never mind the fact that the star herself has said she hasn't had a facelift, though she admitted she wants one eventually and occasionally gets "baby Botox." Speaking to the Cut, she noted the invisible labor that "low-maintenance" women do to appear chill yet also extremely hot.

"I want to be a sexy mom," she said. "At drop-off, I want to look like a woman that has her shit together even when I've just woken up and don't have my shit together."

Despite these revelations, women online felt as if Lawrence was ignoring the elephant in the room: how her face has changed. They began to call out what they saw as a talented, popular and "cool" celebrity giving in to anti-aging culture.

"You can't tell me the patriarchy doesn't exist when the culture we live in and the male gaze is making women's bodies unrecognizable," wrote one person on TikTok.

All of this drama has surpassed the coverage of Mes, the whole reason Lawrence opened herself up to the public in the first place, with tabloids couching the online speculation as " rumors " about what she may have had done.

"Jennifer Lawrence likely underwent multiple plastic surgery procedures costing $30K for 'more youthful' look," read one Page Six headline . A second New York Post story bemoaned the "culture of plastic surgery" that has made famous women "puffed-up, plastic clones."

Why has Lawrence's face sparked so much ire? For some, it's less about what she has or hasn't had done and more about the image she has cultivated of herself and what it means to women writ large.

Writer and brand consultant Natalie Reilly says as much in a recent edition of her Substack newsletter I Say This With Love . "Could it also be that this outrage over Jen's appearance and foray into haircare is really about our semi-conscious desire to have JLaw remain our parasocial TomBoy, down home bestie?" Reilly writes.

Lawrence has always presented herself as a fun and lighthearted girl, the type you might want to have as your best friend. Even the stated purpose of Mes, which is meant to make your hair look great with minimal effort, fits with that same ethos; its slogan is "less time fixing your hair, more time living." If Lawrence can't avoid the constant pressures of the plastic surgery industrial complex — with maintenance Botox in your 20s and deep plane facelifts by 50 — what hope do the rest of us have?

But holding Lawrence to this impossible standard is unfair, Amanda M. Czerniawski, a sociologist and professor at Temple University, tells me. Mainly, because J.Law's face and body are integral to her continued success.

"She's an actress," Czerniawski says. "She is supposed to invest in her body and be an extreme. We as the public are like, Oh no, that is what I should be doing too . But you're not her. That's not your job. But it's blended all together."

Therefore, the overwhelming response to Lawrence's "new face" is really not about her at all, but a symptom of women's general anxiety over the pressures they face. Sure, we expect the Kardashians and the Instagram models to get this and that procedure, but J.Law was supposed to be above all that. Any suggestion that she's not can feel like a personal betrayal.

"Is this now the new standard for the average 36-year-old woman? Like, yeah, you need to get cosmetic surgery and prevent the signs of aging, even though you probably don't really have wrinkles yet?" says Czerniawski. "It's like the bar keeps shifting."

But there are also those women who refuse to take the bait. "Jennifer Lawrence doesn't make me feel pressure about my eyeballs," content creator Jennifer Latch vented in a TikTok calling out the scrutiny the actor has gotten.

"Women can't win," Latch continued. "If we age, it's bad. If we don't age, it's bad. If we do this, it's bad. If we don't do this. … Can we just stop talking about women's bodies?"

articles.title: In 1997, Texas researchers mixed waste printer toner into asphalt; a 10% dose raised the binder grade from PG64-28 to PG70-22 and increased mix strength and stability
articles.summary: In a groundbreaking 1997 study, researchers at the University of Texas at Austin revealed that adding waste printer toner to asphalt significantly improves its strength and stability, raising its binder grade and promising better performance on the roads.
articles.body: In February 1997, researchers at the University of Texas at Austin’s Centre of Transportation Research reported that waste printer toner could be blended into asphalt and make it stiffer and stronger. A 10% dose of toner raised an asphalt binder from PG64-28 to PG70-22; in their tests and mixes made with the modified binder showed higher strength and stability than unmodified ones. The work came out of a cooperative project between the Texas Department of Transportation and the University and its final report is titled Use of Waste Toner in Asphaltic Concrete; Mansour Solaimanian, Thomas W. Kennedy and R.B. McGennis are its authors.Toner went into the binder, not the finished mix Toner’s two primary components are styrene-acrylic copolymer and carbon black, and a TxDOT patent, U.S. Patent 6,113,681, titled Toner-modified asphalt compositions, said both are known to help asphalt. The patent covered compositions with up to 20% toner. It also explained why the order of mixing mattered: toner added after the asphalt and aggregate had been combined tended to act as a filler instead of a modifier. The patent’s preferred method was dry blending the toner into asphalt at least 10°C above the toner’s melting point, which it said was typically about 100 to 150°C depending on the type of toner and it reported the best results when the blending temperature stayed above about 165°C.A 10% dose moved the grade from PG64-28 to PG70-22TxDOT’s summary of the 1997 report says an AC-20 asphalt cement, graded PG64-28 under the Superpave system, grades as PG70-22 with 10% waste toner. The study found that stiffness and viscosity rise as more toner goes into the blend and the increase shows up at high, intermediate and low temperatures. A 1998 paper in the Transportation Research Record, which reported the same research, noted that unused and spent toner was otherwise dumped in landfills. It also carried a caution: the modified binder suited places where rutting was the main worry and where somewhat stiffer behaviour in the cold was not a cracking concern. In North and Central Texas, a PG64-22 binder was expected to perform satisfactorily at 98% reliability and the toner-modified AC-20 met that standard for those regions.Mixes with toner tested stronger and more stableThe researchers put the modified binders into asphalt and aggregate mixtures and measured Hveem stability, resilient modulus and indirect tensile strength. They also ran a Superpave mix design at three toner levels: 0%, 5% and 16% by mass of the binder and toner blend. The mixture analysis showed higher strength and stability for toner-modified asphalt concrete than for unmodified mixtures. Asphalt Magazine’s 2012 review adds that Solaimanian reported the optimum binder content in a Superpave mix design was not affected at a 10% toner level. The report itself ran its mix design at 0%, 5% and 16% and found that toner in the 5% to 16% range did not significantly change the optimum binder content.A Waco highway took 5,000 tons of toner-modified mixThe same year, TxDOT and the Center for Transportation Research completed a field trial in Waco, Texas. Asphalt Magazine reports that 5000 tons of toner-modified hot mix paved two km of a six-lane highway and the road was in excellent condition after about two years, Lora Robosky wrote in Asphalt Magazine’s July 2012 article “Printer and copier toner in asphalt still has jams to consider.” The patent followed in September 2000, according to the same magazine and later test sections went down in the Houston, Laredo and Pharr districts. A 2004 report from the same research centre, Design of Toner Modification for the Houston, Laredo, Pharr and Bryan Demonstration Project, covers the binder design for each site, including blending time, performance grading, storage stability and mixing and companion temperatures.The performance grades of the toner-modified binders varied with the amount of polymer in each toner. The 2004 report by Yetkin Yildirim, Thomas W. Kennedy and Jorge Prozzi found that two hours of blending was enough to get a uniform toner-asphalt mix, but it expected significant storage stability problems regardless of the toner level in the blend. As mentioned in the above study of 1997, stiffness rose with every increase in toner, so the polymer content of each toner mattered for the grade a binder reached. According to TxDOT, additional projects had not been completed, mainly because of the cost of waste toner, the magazine reported.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 'Message to the West': TV channels across Europe receive bomb threats, suspend programming
articles.summary: Television broadcasters across Europe witnessed a Pandemonium on Friday after receiving bomb threats in emails titled 'MESSAGE TO THE WEST', prompting
articles.body: Television broadcasters across Europe witnessed a Pandemonium on Friday after receiving bomb threats in emails titled 'MESSAGE TO THE WEST', prompting evacuations and suspension of programming. The threats were eventually called a hoax.Threats were reported by Irish broadcaster RTE, Britain's Sky and Bulgarian private channel Nova TV, among others. At RTE, some programmes were replaced by music and a pre-recorded message, with the disruption lasting up to three hours.An email received by Nova and RTE warned that an explosive device had been planted inside their buildings and would detonate within 45 minutes."We want the whole world to know about us, which is why one of our operatives has planted an explosive device in your building," the email read. "It will detonate in 45 minutes. The clock is ticking."Police evacuated and searched Nova's newsroom in Sofia before declaring the premises safe. Broadcasting continued uninterrupted, and employees returned to their desks, the broadcaster said. At RTE, staff returned to the campus after police completed a search lasting more than three hours.The threats came amid a series of hoax bomb alerts targeting passenger flights across Europe in recent days. Flights from Serbia to Finland, Spain and other destinations have faced diversions, emergency landings and security checks, although no explosives have been found so far.Friday's incidents also came against the backdrop of growing concerns over hacking scams and cyberattacks in recent weeks, including attacks on supermarkets.The identity of those behind Friday's threats remains unclear. Emails sent to RTE and Nova were signed by Mikhail Andropov, who claimed to be one of the leaders of a group responsible for this week's plane-related hoaxes."But this is only the beginning. What happened this week is just a small part of what awaits Europe in the near future," the message added.The purported sender shared a surname with Yuri Andropov, a former General Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union. The email's title, “MESSAGE TO THE WEST”, also echoed the title of a biography of the former Soviet leader, “New Challenge to the West”.It remains unclear whether these references point to Russian involvement or were intended to direct suspicion towards Moscow.Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin said European security agencies had not yet established whether the threats targeting air travel and media organisations were being made by individuals or were part of a coordinated attack."It just illustrates how relatively simple it can be to cause disruption and to undermine the normal operation of society through unconventional activities of this kind, which are designed to cause disruption, designed to cause fear and anxiety," Martin told RTE radio shortly after news programming resumed from an outside broadcasting unit."We have to remain calm," he added.You use AI every day. articles.title: ‘100% in favour of Super Intelligence’: Trump backs AI expansion despite growing data centre backlash
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump has backed the expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) across the country, saying his administration will work with states
articles.body: US President Donald Trump has backed the expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) across the country, saying his administration will work with states seeking to attract investment in what he described as "Super Intelligence (SI)", even as growing local opposition threatens to slow the industry's rapid expansion.In a post on Truth Social on Friday, November 6, Trump argued that states embracing advanced AI technology could reap significant economic benefits and warned that rejecting such investments would be a mistake."As President, I am 100% in favor of Super Intelligence (SI), and will work with the many States in the U.S. that want to become RICH by having them. They are GOLD, and only foolish leadership will say 'NO' to the riches they bring!" he wrote.Trump's remarks come days after voters in several parts of the country backed measures seeking to restrict or temporarily halt data centre construction, highlighting rising concerns about the impact of the AI boom on local communities.Growing resistance to AI infrastructure expansionAccording to Axios, nearly two dozen of 41 data centre-related ballot measures across 10 states appeared headed for approval based on preliminary results from Tuesday's midterm elections. Several of these measures sought restrictions or temporary pauses on new construction.The resistance reflects concerns that the rapid expansion of data centres, which require enormous amounts of electricity and water, could increase utility bills, strain local resources and affect the environment.The election results could complicate plans for an estimated $10 trillion expansion of AI infrastructure in the United States.Texas, expected to account for 41 per cent of new US data centre capacity in 2028, according to research firm SemiAnalysis cited by Axios, could face particular challenges.Democrat Gina Hinojosa's victory over Republican Governor Greg Abbott has also raised questions about the future of data centre development in the state. Hinojosa campaigned on maintaining a moratorium on new data centres until lawmakers address concerns involving electricity, water supplies, air quality and property rights.Democrats also won gubernatorial contests in Ohio, Georgia and Arizona, three other states expected to play significant roles in the country's AI infrastructure expansion.Trump wants data centres to address local concernsTrump has previously sought to address concerns over the impact of large data centres while continuing to encourage investment in the sector.In an October 20 Truth Social post, he said major data centres should generate their own electricity, sell excess power to local utilities and provide financial benefits to nearby residents."MAKE DEALS, and get them built!!! GREAT FOR THE US," he wrote.The president has also established a federal Super Intelligence Force to help maintain America's technological leadership.Meanwhile, the Associated Press reported on Friday that voters had overwhelmingly supported local restrictions on data centres, underlining the political challenges facing the administration's AI expansion plans.Trump's latest comments indicate that he intends to continue backing the development of advanced AI and the infrastructure supporting it, despite growing resistance from communities and local leaders concerned about its economic and environmental costs.You use AI every day. articles.title: PM Modi, Rahul Gandhi & Trump on Apple's secret word graylist: Report
articles.summary: A researcher has discovered an undisclosed multilingual list containing tens of thousands of words and phrases that Apple’s iOS keyboard avoids suggesting
articles.body: A researcher has discovered an undisclosed multilingual list containing tens of thousands of words and phrases that Apple’s iOS keyboard avoids suggesting through autocomplete and swipe-typing, Reuters reported.Derek Kauffman, the researcher who uncovered the list, described it as a “very light-touch form of censorship.” However, he cautioned that given the scale of Apple’s operations, “it only takes a light touch to have a big impact.”The list does not constitute a formal ban. iPhone users can still manually type any words or phrases in their emails and messages. The restriction simply means that, in most cases, the keyboard will not suggest these terms through predictive text or swipe-to-type features.Which words and phrases are on the listMost of the flagged words and phrases are vulgar, offensive or related to drugs, sex and violence. However, the list also includes politically sensitive terms such as “dictator Trump” and “sleepy Joe,” referring to US President Donald Trump and his predecessor, Joe Biden. Trump has repeatedly mocked Biden as "sleepy Joe."Other phrases excluded from iOS's predictive text features include “right wing conspiracy,” “Tibetan independence” and “United Ireland.” The list also has an India connection.Different languages have their own set of flagged words and phrases. In Hindi, for instance, the keyboard does not allow users to swipe-type references to Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Rahul Gandhi, the Lok Sabha leader of the opposition.Similarly, French speakers cannot swipe-type the phrase “immigration too high,” while Hebrew speakers face restrictions on the phrase “occupied territories.”“Every major language has some version of this,” Kauffman told Reuters. While acknowledging that Apple may be trying to prevent users from accidentally sending obscene messages or inflammatory slogans, he highlighted what he described as "inconsistencies" in how the company applies the feature.As an example, he pointed to the word “smut,” which means a sexually explicit material. He said users could swipe-type “read smut” but not “read gay smut.”How the list was discoveredKauffman discovered the list in September after noticing that swipe-typing — gliding a finger across the keyboard to enter words — would stutter over certain phrases, such as “bad boy” and “white man,” but not “bad girl” or “black man.”Curious about the pattern, he used OpenAI’s Codex and Anthropic’s Claude Code to investigate, eventually uncovering a list stored in a location he described as “deep in the bowels” of Apple's operating system. While the count varies depending on how word combinations and their permutations are calculated, Kauffman estimated that there are around 100,000 entries, excluding Chinese characters.Reuters independently corroborated his findings, with phrases such as “United Ireland” and “Sleepy Joe” failing swipe-typing tests.Separately, Matt Suiche, an engineer at agentic AI cybersecurity company Tolmo, recovered the same list and cross-checked Kauffman's findings against Apple's internal data, obtaining a near-perfect match.Suiche noted that the list had been hidden in plain sight for years, offering an insight into how “human communication has been potentially influenced and filtered for years inside messaging apps.”Why the list raises transparency concernsUsers have questioned iOS's predictive text restrictions for years, with several taking to social media to highlight phrases they could not swipe-type. Earlier this week, a Norwegian systems administrator independently uncovered a list of flagged words, including “al-Qaeda,” “Auschwitz” and “Hooters.”However, the existence of a much broader list of sensitive phrases is a first.Apple is not the only tech company to face scrutiny over predictive text. Alphabet-owned Google has repeatedly faced criticism, and even lawsuits, over controversial autocomplete suggestions.Apple, too, drew attention last year when users reported that dictating the word “racist” on their iPhones briefly caused the word “Trump” to appear on screen. The company attributed the issue to an error and said it had been fixed.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A Texas mother moved to Portugal while her teenage children stayed with their father; after years of custody appeals, a court upheld a plan granting her summer and school-holiday visits, plus at least two calls each week
articles.summary: A Texas appeals court has upheld an updated custody arrangement between a mother living in Portugal and a father living in Texas.
articles.body: A Texas appeals court has upheld an updated custody arrangement between a mother living in Portugal and a father living in Texas. The decision brings an end to years of legal disputes over parental access to their two teenage children. The Texas Third Court of Appeals issued a written decision confirming a lower court's order that gives the mother a clear visitation schedule. Under the approved plan, the mother will have custody of the children during summer breaks, spring breaks, and alternating major holidays. She will also have regular weekly phone and electronic contact with them during the school year, when the teenagers live with their father in Texas.Origin of the legal disputeThe legal dispute began after the parents divorced in 2012. At first, they shared joint custody while living in Texas. In 2022, the mother accepted a place in a PhD programme in Portugal and asked the court to change the custody agreement. She wanted to remove the rules limiting where the children could live. She also asked for permission to obtain passports for the children. The father later filed his own request, asking the court to give him primary physical custody. He also wanted strict rules for any international visits by the children. After a hearing, a Hays County district court changed the children's primary residence to the father's home. However, the court created a flexible visitation plan based on agreements between the parents and the teenagers' personal schedules. The mother appealed that first decision. She argued that relying on informal agreements made her visitation rights unclear and difficult to enforce legally. The appeals court agreed with her in an earlier ruling. It instructed the district court to prepare a clear schedule that listed the dates and conditions for her time with the children and her communication with them.District court establishes detailed scheduleFollowing the appeals court's instructions, the district court held further proceedings to create a clear visitation schedule. The new plan took international travel and the children's school calendars into account. Under the final order, the mother received specific summer visitation rights. Her time with the children would begin shortly after the school year ended and finish before classes started again in August. She was also given set periods during holiday breaks. To help her stay in regular contact with the children despite the distance between the two countries, the court ordered weekly telephone calls during the school year. The trial judge also appointed an attorney to prepare the formal court order based on these terms. The mother objected to this process and also challenged the decision about how court costs should be divided. These objections led to a second appeal.Appellate court affirms rulingIn its latest decision, the Texas Third Court of Appeals rejected the mother's challenges to the district court's procedures and the visitation schedule. The appeals court found that the district court had acted within its legal powers when it created a clear and enforceable visitation plan. The judges said the arrangement balanced the mother's decision to move to Europe with the teenagers' need for educational and social stability in Texas. The court also found that the set summer visits, holiday breaks, and weekly telephone contact provided enough protection for the mother's parental rights while keeping the children's best interests at the centre of the decision.You use AI every day. articles.title: Paris built a 427-kilometre underground postal network powered by compressed air, delivering millions of letters and telegrams across the city in about two hours before maintenance problems led to its closure in 1984
articles.summary: Paris once operated the world's largest pneumatic postal network, stretching 427 kilometres beneath the city's streets by 1933.
articles.body: Paris once operated the world's largest pneumatic postal network, stretching 427 kilometres beneath the city's streets by 1933. Using compressed air, the underground system transported messages and letters in special containers between post offices, delivering correspondence in approximately two hours. Originally developed to speed up telegram transmission, the network opened to public correspondence in 1879 and became an important part of Parisian communications. However, ageing infrastructure, rising maintenance difficulties and the growing use of telephones, telex and fax gradually reduced its importance. After more than a century of operation, the pneumatic postal service was discontinued on March 30, 1984.How did Paris's pneumatic postal network use compressed airAccording to the Committee for the History of the Post Office (CHP), the pneumatic postal network used compressed air to move containers carrying messages through underground tubes. These containers, known as cursors, travelled between connected postal and telegraph offices. The Paris system initially relied on water-powered equipment to produce compressed air, rather than the vacuum-based method used in London. According to the CHP's historical account, the administration later introduced steam-powered machinery in 1871 and gradually extended its use across the network from 1879. The system was subsequently improved through changes to its machinery, tubes and terminals to accommodate increasing numbers of dispatches.A major development came on January 25, 1879, when the administration established a public pneumatic postal service. Until then, the network had primarily supported the transmission of telegrams. Following this decision, members of the public could send open or closed forms through the service, while express letters were introduced in 1898. The network was extended across the Paris districts, and additional staff were employed to manage the growing volume of correspondence. According to the CHP publication, delivery to recipients generally took approximately two hours, making the service particularly useful for businesses, government offices and people who needed messages delivered quickly.How large was Paris's pneumatic postal network by 1933By 1933, the Paris pneumatic postal network had reached 427 kilometres of underground tubes, making it the largest network of its kind in the world. It connected postal offices across the capital and supported the movement of messages through a system of interconnected routes. The network was not limited to a small number of central offices; it had become an established part of the city's communications infrastructure. According to the CHP publication, the service was profitable at the time and employed specialised staff responsible for loading, transmitting and distributing dispatches, as well as maintaining the machinery.The network continued to serve Paris during the 20th century and experienced a significant increase in use during the Second World War. The CHP publication records that the volume of items transported increased from four million in 1940 to 16 million in 1945. However, the system gradually faced technical and financial difficulties. Although improvements were introduced, including the electrification of machinery and experiments with automated operations, these changes were not implemented across the entire network. Plastic tubes, which offered advantages over the earlier steel versions, also began replacing them only from 1965 and through occasional interventions.Why did Paris's pneumatic postal network begin to declineThe decline of the pneumatic postal network became increasingly apparent during the 1970s and early 1980s. According to the CHP publication, blockages involving the moving containers became more frequent, while maintenance problems left large sections of the network unusable. By 1983, slightly more than half of the lines could no longer operate. In areas where the underground system was unavailable, correspondence had to be transported above ground using cyclists or motorcyclists. The cost of maintaining and renewing the extensive infrastructure also became increasingly difficult to justify as the volume of mail carried by the network declined.The growing availability of alternative communication technologies further contributed to the decline. Telephone communications expanded, while telex and fax services became increasingly accessible to businesses that had previously relied on pneumatic deliveries. The volume of pneumatic dispatches fell from four million at the beginning of the 1960s to 2.7 million in 1973 and 650,000 in 1982. The service was eventually discontinued on March 30, 1984, at 5 pm, bringing an end to the Paris-wide pneumatic postal network. Some independent pneumatic systems continued operating at locations such as La Salpêtrière Hospital, the Paris-Favorites postal cheque centre and the National Assembly.You use AI every day. articles.title: Fears Starlink, builds one of its own: Russia rushes to scale up Rassvet
articles.summary: Russia's Security Council on Friday called for an urgent expansion of the country's homegrown satellite internet network, warning that Elon Musk's
articles.body: Russia's Security Council on Friday called for an urgent expansion of the country's homegrown satellite internet network, warning that Elon Musk's Starlink system could be used to destabilise society and politics in unspecified sovereign states.The push to accelerate the development of Rassvet, Russia's answer to Starlink, comes as Moscow is already using the nascent network for military communications in Ukraine.Ukraine's military intelligence directorate (GUR) told Reuters that Russia was using Rassvet to support military communications and improve the accuracy of its strike drones while making them harder to jam. However, the network's coverage remains limited, with communications available only intermittently as satellites pass over relevant areas.Russia has launched 32 Rassvet satellites into orbit so far this year in two batches, in March and July, according to GUR. The Russian government had said last month that it had launched more than 30 satellites as part of the low-Earth orbit network."The constellation is currently insufficient to provide uninterrupted coverage of Ukrainian territory: communication is available intermittently when the satellites pass over the relevant areas," GUR spokesman Andrii Yusov said in a written statement, Reuters reported."Russia is using the 'Rassvet' satellite system over the territory of ⁠Ukraine for military purposes," he added.Moscow plans to carry out further Rassvet launches by the end of 2026 to extend the network's geographical coverage and gradually move towards a fully operational low-orbit satellite communications system, GUR said.Russia seeks expanding Starlink alternativeOn Friday, Moscow's Security Council called for an urgent expansion of the country's satellite communications capabilities, warning that Western services such as Starlink and OneWeb could pose security risks to unspecified sovereign states, Reuters reported."To boost the development of the (Rassvet) system, it is necessary to rapidly scale up the mass production of communications satellites and terminal equipment," the Security Council said in a statement, according to Russian state media.The council added that relevant government agencies had been instructed to prepare proposals to ensure the full-scale deployment and sustainable operation of the network.The warning came after a meeting of the praesidium of the Security Council's Scientific and Expert Council, which discussed information security and internet access. During the meeting, officials highlighted what they described as the risks posed by Western satellite communication networks operating over sovereign territories."During the meeting, the main risks and threats posed by the use of Western space-based communications systems over the territory of sovereign states to destabilise the socio-political situation were highlighted. This applies, first and foremost, to the widely used satellite communications services Starlink and OneWeb," state media quoted the council's statement as saying, Reuters reported.Russian President Vladimir Putin last month acknowledged that the country was only beginning to develop its alternative to Starlink, while describing Musk as a genius.By comparison, Starlink has more than 10,000 active satellites. Its military version has been used extensively by Ukrainian forces during the war, particularly for drone operations and battlefield communications. Access to SpaceX's satellite network, which Moscow does not have, has provided Kyiv with a significant advantage in the conflict.

articles.title: An Arkansas couple bought property together in 2021 and divorced less than a year later, each keeping half; after the woman remarried and filed for bankruptcy, a court dismissed his challenge to the sale of her share
articles.summary: A federal appeals court has upheld the sale of a divorced woman's half-share in a property in Arkansas.
articles.body: A federal appeals court has upheld the sale of a divorced woman's half-share in a property in Arkansas. The court rejected a legal challenge from her former husband, who tried to stop the sale after she filed for bankruptcy. The United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit ruled on 4 November 2026 to uphold an earlier decision dismissing an appeal by Logan Riffenburg. The ruling allows the Chapter 7 bankruptcy trustee to complete the sale of the property share to Blue Sun Capital LLC, ending a legal dispute between the former couple that lasted several years. According to court documents published by Justia, the dispute began in August 2021, when Riffenburg and his then-wife, Vanessa Roper, jointly bought a property in Mountain View, Arkansas. The couple divorced less than a year later. As part of the divorce, each received an equal half-share of the property.Bankruptcy filing triggers estate saleAfter the divorce, Roper remarried and later filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy protection with her new husband, Billy Joe Roper Jr, in March 2023. Under federal bankruptcy law, a Chapter 7 trustee is appointed to manage the debtor's assets and use them to repay creditors. The appointed trustee, Mark Randy Rice, asked the United States Bankruptcy Court for the Eastern District of Arkansas for permission to sell Roper's half-share in the Mountain View property to Blue Sun Capital LLC. He made the request under Section 363(b) of the Bankruptcy Code. Riffenburg objected to the planned sale. He tried to stop the trustee from transferring his former wife's share of the property to an outside investment company. The bankruptcy court rejected Riffenburg's objection and found that the trustee had acted properly. The court said the trustee was carrying out his legal duty to sell the assets in the bankruptcy estate in good faith, at a fair price, and in the best interests of everyone involved.Legal fight over good-faith purchaser rulesAfter the bankruptcy court approved the sale, Riffenburg appealed to the Bankruptcy Appellate Panel for the Eighth Circuit. However, he did not obtain a court order to pause the sale while his appeal was being considered. Since there was no order stopping the transaction, Trustee Rice completed the sale of the half-share to Blue Sun Capital LLC. He then asked the court to dismiss Riffenburg's appeal under Section 363(m) of the Bankruptcy Code, arguing that the appeal had become legally moot. Section 363(m), which federal courts often call the finality rule, protects completed bankruptcy sales. It states that a court cannot reverse or change an approved sale on appeal if the buyer acted in good faith, unless the person challenging the sale had first obtained a court order to stop the transaction while the appeal was pending. A divided panel of the Bankruptcy Appellate Panel accepted the trustee's request and dismissed the appeal. Riffenburg then took the case to the Eighth Circuit. He argued that the finality rule should not apply because the bankruptcy court had never clearly ruled that Blue Sun Capital LLC was a good-faith buyer.Appeals court relies on established precedentWriting for the three-judge appeals panel, Circuit Judge Raymond Gruender explained that Riffenburg had failed to raise concerns about the buyer's good faith during the original bankruptcy court proceedings. This failure was enough to defeat his appeal. "At no point in the bankruptcy-court proceedings did Riffenburg argue that Blue Sun Capital was not a good-faith purchaser of Roper's interest in the Arkansas property," Circuit Judge Gruender wrote in the majority opinion. "Under our precedent, Riffenburg's failure to challenge Blue Sun Capital's good faith in the bankruptcy court is dispositive." The Eighth Circuit relied on a previous 2001 ruling, In re Rodriquez. That case established that someone who objects to a bankruptcy sale loses the right to challenge the buyer's good faith during an appeal if they did not raise the issue before the trial judge. In this case, Riffenburg had only challenged the trustee's legal authority to sell the property share. He had not questioned the buyer's actions or good faith. As a result, the appeals court found that the legal protections provided by the finality rule still applied. The panel also considered Riffenburg's argument about a 2023 United States Supreme Court decision, MOAC Mall Holdings LLC v. Transform Holdco LLC. He claimed that the ruling had changed the Eighth Circuit's earlier rules on appeals involving bankruptcy sales. The appeals court explained that the Supreme Court had clarified that Section 363(m) does not automatically prevent a court from hearing an appeal because of a lack of jurisdiction. However, the requirement to raise concerns about a buyer's good faith before the trial court remained established law in the Eighth Circuit. While agreeing with the dismissal, the appeals panel added a note in a footnote that some judges had doubts about whether the circuit's strict rule on raising objections was fully consistent with the actual wording of Section 363(m). However, the court said it was required to follow its earlier decisions. The ruling means the sale of the Mountain View property share to Blue Sun Capital LLC remains completed and legally final.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 1959, the US Navy fired a guided missile from a submarine carrying 3,000 letters; it reached Florida in 22 minutes, but the experiment never became a postal service
articles.summary: On a June morning in 1959, a US Navy submarine became an unusual starting point for a postal delivery.
articles.body: On a June morning in 1959, a US Navy submarine became an unusual starting point for a postal delivery. Instead of loading its mail onto an aircraft or a conventional transport vehicle, the Navy placed thousands of letters inside a guided missile and launched it towards Florida. The journey took just 22 minutes as reported by Smithsonian National Postal Museum. The operation involved the USS Barbero, a Regulus I cruise missile and 3,000 pieces of mail intended for delivery at a naval air station near Jacksonville. It was presented as a demonstration of how military technology might serve a civilian purpose. Yet the experiment, despite attracting considerable attention, never developed into a regular method of transporting mail.How a US Navy submarine launched a missile carrying 3,000 lettersThe vessel chosen for the operation was the USS Barbero, a US Navy submarine equipped to launch Regulus I guided missiles. During the Cold War, the Navy had been developing submarine-based missile systems as part of its wider military strategy. The Regulus was designed to travel considerable distances under guidance, carrying a nuclear warhead if required. For the 1959 demonstration, however, its payload was rather different.Two specially prepared metal containers were fitted into the missile before launch. They held a combined total of 3,000 letters. Their red and blue paintwork reflected the colours commonly associated with American postal boxes, while the words "US Mail" identified their intended purpose.The containers occupied the section of the missile normally reserved for its nuclear payload. It was a temporary change to the missile's usual configuration, allowing the Navy to demonstrate a non-military application of the same delivery system.The operation also involved Arthur Summerfield, who was serving as the US Postmaster General.The 22-minute missile flight that delivered 3,000 letters to FloridaThe launch took place on June 8, 1959. Shortly before noon, the Regulus I was fired from the USS Barbero and sent towards the Naval Auxiliary Air Station at Mayport, Florida, close to Jacksonville. The distance between the submarine and its destination was approximately 100 miles. The missile completed the journey in 22 minutes before reaching the designated naval facility.For a postal experiment, the delivery method was far removed from the established network of trucks, trains, ships and aircraft used by the US Postal Service. The letters had travelled inside a weapon originally developed for military operations, guided towards a predetermined destination by sophisticated navigation equipment.The flight demonstrated that a missile could carry a relatively small payload over a considerable distance and reach a specified location with precision.The 1959 vision of sending international letters aboard guided missilesSummerfield viewed the demonstration as an opportunity to explore faster ways of moving correspondence across long distances. At the time, the development of guided missiles was progressing alongside wider advances in aviation, communications and space technology. He believed that the accuracy and speed of these systems could eventually have applications in civilian postal transportation. The Florida flight gave him an occasion to discuss that possibility publicly.Following the successful delivery, Summerfield described the operation as the first official use of a guided missile to carry mail by a national postal department. He also made a prediction about how the technology might develop. He suggested that, before humans reached the Moon, guided missiles could be transporting letters between New York and California, as well as to destinations such as Britain, India and Australia, with journeys taking only a few hours.The Cold War technology behind the deliveryThe Regulus I was developed as a guided cruise missile for the US Navy. Its purpose was to give submarines the ability to launch a nuclear-capable weapon towards targets hundreds of miles away. Its guidance system was designed to direct the missile along a planned course. The 1959 postal flight used that capability on a much shorter journey, covering roughly 100 miles between the submarine and Mayport.The choice of a missile was significant in the context of the Cold War. Both the United States and the Soviet Union were investing heavily in military technology, including long-range weapons and delivery systems. Demonstrating the accuracy of American missile technology also carried a wider strategic message. The mail operation therefore had two dimensions. Publicly, it was presented as an experiment in transporting correspondence. At the same time, it provided a demonstration of the Navy's ability to guide a missile towards a specific destination.Why missile mail never became a postal serviceDespite the successful flight and Summerfield's predictions, the experiment was not repeated as an American postal operation. The June 1959 launch remained the only known instance of the US Postal Service using a guided missile to transport mail. The demonstration established that letters could be carried from a submarine to a designated location using missile technology. It did not establish that the method could compete with existing postal transportation systems.A regular service would have required specialised equipment, launch facilities, carefully planned routes and substantial coordination between military and postal authorities. The cost and practical demands of using military missiles for routine correspondence also raised questions about whether such a system would offer meaningful advantages.Its place in postal history is preserved through objects associated with the flight. The Smithsonian National Postal Museum holds a Regulus I missile mail container from the demonstration, documenting the unusual attempt to combine military technology with civilian mail delivery.The day a submarine became a post officeThe USS Barbero's 1959 mission lasted only 22 minutes, but it created one of the more unusual episodes in American postal history. Three thousand letters travelled inside a guided missile, launched from beneath the surface of the sea and delivered to a naval facility in Florida.The experiment took place at a time when military and technological developments were prompting new ideas about long-distance transportation. Summerfield's vision of missile-powered mail never materialised, and conventional postal networks continued to handle the movement of letters.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: John Wick star Keanu Reeves offered a stranger a 15-minute Zoom date during Covid; the unusual fundraiser was organised to help a children's cancer charity after its biggest annual event was cancelled
articles.summary: Hollywood actor Keanu Reeves found an unusual way to support children battling cancer during the Covid-19 pandemic in 2020.
articles.body: Hollywood actor Keanu Reeves found an unusual way to support children battling cancer during the Covid-19 pandemic in 2020. The John Wick star offered a private 15-minute Zoom conversation to the highest bidder as part of an online fundraising initiative organised by Camp Rainbow Gold, an Idaho-based charity supporting children diagnosed with cancer and their families. The initiative came after the organisation was forced to cancel its biggest annual fundraising event, the Share Your Heart Ball, with just 48 hours' notice because of the pandemic. With traditional fundraising opportunities disrupted, the charity turned to online bidding and invited celebrities and businesses to contribute experiences that supporters could compete to win.Keanu Reeves offered a private 15-minute Zoom conversationThe experience, titled 15 Minutes of Fame with Keanu Reeves, gave one successful bidder the opportunity to speak privately with the actor over Zoom. According to Camp Rainbow Gold's announcement on June 11, 2020, Reeves was willing to share a virtual glass of wine, tell stories, answer questions and even teach a few karate moves during the conversation.The offer was part of the charity's Shine for Camp online fundraising initiative. The organisation described the opportunity as a chance to connect with the actor from home, at a time when pandemic restrictions had made in-person meetings difficult.The call was scheduled for the week beginning July 6, 2020, at a mutually agreed time.Covid forced the charity to cancel its biggest annual fundraiserCamp Rainbow Gold had planned to hold its annual Share Your Heart Ball, one of its primary fundraising events, but the rapidly spreading coronavirus forced it to call off the event just two days before it was due to take place.The cancellation created a major challenge for the Idaho nonprofit. Its executive director, Elizabeth Lizberg, said the organisation quickly recognised that other charities were also moving their fundraising activities online. The team decided to create an online fundraiser featuring experiences and contributions from celebrities, businesses and other supporters.The initiative was designed to raise money while offering people a way to connect and participate in fundraising without meeting in person.Bidding for the Keanu Reeves experience crossed $16,000The opportunity to spend 15 minutes with Reeves attracted considerable attention. When Entertainment Tonight reported on the initiative on June 16, 2020, the highest bid had reached $16,200. A day later, CNN reported that bidding had climbed to $16,600, with the offer initially carrying an estimated value of $10,000.The bidding was scheduled to close on June 22, 2020. The money raised through the initiative was intended to support Camp Rainbow Gold and its work with children diagnosed with cancer and their families.Other celebrities also contributed to the online fundraiserReeves was not the only entertainer who offered a personal experience for the charity's online initiative. Singer Ally Brooke, formerly of Fifth Harmony, contributed a private 15-minute Zoom mini-concert. Voice actor Rob Paulsen offered a one-hour experience in which the winner could get advice on voice acting, along with signed merchandise and a recorded voicemail message.The fundraiser also featured contributions from businesses and other supporters, including holiday and travel experiences. The mix of celebrity encounters and other offerings helped the charity move its fundraising efforts online after the cancellation of its annual event.What Camp Rainbow Gold does for children with cancerCamp Rainbow Gold is an Idaho-based nonprofit whose work centres on providing emotionally empowering experiences for children diagnosed with cancer and their families. Its programmes have included camps and activities for young patients, their siblings and family members.The organisation's work also recognises that a cancer diagnosis affects more than the child receiving treatment. By creating opportunities for children and families to spend time together and connect with others facing similar circumstances, the charity aims to provide support beyond medical care.The pandemic disrupted the organisation's usual activities and fundraising plans, but it continued working to reach the families it served. The online fundraiser featuring Reeves was one of the ways it sought to keep that support going during an exceptionally difficult period.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: In March 2026, Meryl Streep made a seven-figure gift to a women's history museum; on November 6, it is set to honour two teachers whose campaign for a new AP history course has backing from 100 universities
articles.summary: Two high school history teachers from California are set to receive the first Meryl Streep Educator Award at a national awards gala on 6 November 2026.
articles.body: Two high school history teachers from California are set to receive the first Meryl Streep Educator Award at a national awards gala on 6 November 2026. The award recognises their work to create the first Advanced Placement course focused entirely on American women's history. The award ceremony will take place in Chicago. It follows a major donation worth seven figures that actor Meryl Streep made to the National Women's History Museum in March 2026. The donation aims to expand the museum's educational programmes and digital learning resources. According to announcements from PR Newswire and the National Women's History Museum, Kristen Kelly and Serene Williams, teachers at Sacred Heart Preparatory in Atherton, California, were selected for their work to develop an Advanced Placement U.S. Women's History course. The course is informally known as WAPUSH. Their campaign has received official support from 100 universities and colleges across the United States.National recognition at Chicago galaThe award will be presented during the museum's 15th annual Women Making History Awards Gala. Streep, who is the honorary chair of the 2026 event, created the educator award to recognise teachers who include women's contributions to history in everyday high school lessons. Along with Kelly and Williams, this year's award recipients and honourees include civil rights pioneer Ruby Bridges, sports executive Laura Ricketts, the U.S. Women's National Hockey Team, business founder Gregg Renfrew, and law firm ArentFox Schiff. The National Women's History Museum was founded in 1996 as an educational organisation that mainly operates online. It is hosting the event as part of the country's preparations for the 250th anniversary of the United States. In press materials released by the museum, President and Chief Executive Officer Frédérique Irwin spoke about the importance of including different voices in history education and making learning opportunities available to everyone. "From Ruby Bridges' courage to ArentFox Schiff's longstanding partnership and Kristen Kelly and Serene Williams' leadership in transforming history education, this year's honorees demonstrate that preserving and expanding opportunity begins with ensuring every generation has access to the full American story," Irwin said.Grassroots campaign gains university supportKelly and Williams began working on the proposed course at Sacred Heart Preparatory because they believed that traditional high school history programmes were missing an important part of American history. Under the current Advanced Placement programme managed by the College Board, high school students can take specialised courses in European History, World History, African American History, and Art History. However, there is no separate Advanced Placement course dedicated to women's history. To show that colleges and universities were interested in the subject, Kelly and Williams started a nationwide campaign. Their goal was to get higher education institutions to recognise the proposed course and offer college credit or suitable course placement to students who completed it. According to information released by Sacred Heart Schools, Atherton, the campaign reached an important milestone after receiving written support from 100 colleges and universities. These endorsements confirm that the participating institutions would accept course credits or offer students suitable placement after completing the proposed curriculum. The course will use original historical research, old records, and legal documents to explore women's leadership, work, and social movements throughout North American history.Philanthropic backing expands classroom reachThe creation of the educator award is directly linked to the expanded work made possible by Streep's financial support for the museum. In March 2026, the museum announced that Streep had made a major donation worth seven figures. The money will help create digital learning materials for classrooms, training programmes for teachers, and online exhibitions. These resources are designed to reach schools across the country. Speaking about the importance of historical stories and preserving culture, Irwin explained the long-term purpose of the donation."Meryl Streep understands that storytelling shapes culture, and culture shapes what societies believe is possible," Irwin said in statements reported by The Times of India. "Her remarkable gift allows us to meet this moment with urgency and imagination, reaching new generations with stories that inspire confidence, ambition, and progress."Speaking about her continued support for the museum, Streep also highlighted the importance of keeping accurate historical records for future generations."The National Women's History Museum has long been a catalyst for bringing forward the stories that deepen our understanding of who we are," Streep said in statements reported by The Story Exchange. "I am proud to continue supporting this essential work so that future generations inherit a history that is both truthful and complete."The 6 November gala in Chicago will also raise money for the museum's digital educational resources and programmes that provide support to teachers. Ticket proceeds will help fund these efforts and expand access to women's history education.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: British Hindu boy, 9, through his father, sues former primary school for not allowing him to wear tilak-chandlo
articles.summary: LONDON: The father of a nine-year-old British Indian Hindu boy is suing his son’s former primary school in the high court, King’s Bench Division, for
articles.body: LONDON: The father of a nine-year-old British Indian Hindu boy is suing his son’s former primary school in the high court, King’s Bench Division, for unlawful religious discrimination and harassment for not allowing him to wear a tilak-chandlo at school, a manifestation of his Hindu Swaminarayan faith.The father, funded by UK Hindu network Action for Harmony, as his son’s “litigation friend”, is seeking £25,000 in damages from the governing body of Vicar’s Green primary school in Alperton, a state school in Ealing borough, also claiming breach of public sector equality duty and interference with the boy’s Article 9 (freedom of religion) and Article 14 (prohibiting discrimination) ECHR rights.In the court papers, which TOI has seen, the father alleges that in Nov 2025 the child, then eight, was questioned about his tilak-chandlo by staff and told it was not permitted.His parents wrote to the school saying their son had worn it for four years and there was nothing in the school’s uniform policy prohibiting it. On Dec 12 the boy was removed from the school council, where he was a representative of his class. Next the school issued a new uniform policy prohibiting religious symbols. In Jan 2026 the parents withdrew their child from the school.The school, in its defence, disputes the whole claim, denying it unlawfully discriminated against the boy. “The prohibition on wearing the tilak-chandlo on the claimant’s forehead did not prevent him from practising Hinduism,” the school claims, adding “there were legitimate concerns that acceding to the claimant’s wearing of the tilak-chandlo… might have significant adverse consequences, including a breakdown in pupil cohesiveness”.The school questions whether the boy follows the Swaminarayan Hindu faith, “denies that it is obligatory to daily wear the mark on the middle of the forehead”, and alleges staff suggested the boy wear the symbol “on parts of his body that are covered”, which his parents rejected.Ambrish Limbachia, director of Ashray Law, representing the boy through his father, said: “This case raises important questions about religious freedom and equality in British education.”You use AI every day. articles.title: Singer Jewel helped build a youth foundation focused on mental health; its free online tools have reached more than 1.6 million users, while 95% of its leadership students earned college scholarship offers
articles.summary: Singer-songwriter Jewel has helped develop a youth-focused mental health programme that combines emotional wellbeing, education and practical life skills,
articles.body: Singer-songwriter Jewel has helped develop a youth-focused mental health programme that combines emotional wellbeing, education and practical life skills, reaching people far beyond its original community in Las Vegas. Through the Inspiring Children Foundation and its initiative, young people and families can access free online resources designed to help them manage difficult emotions and build healthier relationships. The foundation says its digital mental health tools have reached more than 1.6 million users, while 95% of students in its leadership programme have received college scholarship offers for academic achievement and athletics.Jewel's youth foundation combines mental health support with educationThe Inspiring Children Foundation, a non-profit organisation based in Las Vegas, has spent more than 25 years supporting young people facing difficult circumstances. The organisation works with children and families from different socio-economic backgrounds, helping them address challenges involving anxiety, depression, suicidal thoughts and other mental health concerns.Its approach extends beyond conventional educational support. The foundation describes its work as a whole-human programme, bringing together physical, social, emotional and mental health rather than treating these areas separately.The organisation uses mentoring, tennis, entrepreneurship, leadership development and project-based learning to engage young people. The foundation says it serves hundreds of young people in person and reaches millions online. Its leadership programme includes approximately 150 students, while its approach is being replicated by non-profit organisations in 22 cities.What is Jewel Never Broken and how does it support young peopleJewel Never Broken is a mental health initiative developed through a partnership between the singer and the Inspiring Children Foundation. The programme draws on Jewel's own experiences of hardship and recovery, translating lessons from her life into practical resources for young people.Its curriculum offers children tools Jewel used during her journey from homelessness to happiness. Its central aim is to help participants develop different aspects of themselves and become what the organisation calls whole humans.The initiative also supports families with essential resources to encourage their growth. Rather than concentrating exclusively on academic performance or individual achievements, it aims to help young people make healthier choices and develop a stronger understanding of themselves.Jewel, a four-time Grammy-nominated singer-songwriter and two-time New York Times bestselling author, has helped bring these practices to a wider audience through the foundation's online platform.Free digital resources make mental health support accessibleOne of the programme's major developments has been its expansion through online tools. The foundation says websites associated with Jewel Never Broken have provided physical, emotional and mental health resources to more than 1.6 million users.These resources include mindfulness exercises designed to encourage reflection, gratitude and greater awareness of everyday thoughts. The foundation highlights practices such as paying attention, expressing gratitude and retraining the brain as ways of helping people develop more constructive habits.Free resources allow individuals from different locations to explore the practices without joining a physical programme.The website also provides access to a mental health community and online activities intended to help people feel connected. This digital approach is particularly important for individuals who may not have easy access to supportive programmes in their own communities.How young people help create mental health resourcesAn important feature of the Inspiring Children Foundation's work is that young people are not simply recipients of support. They also help develop and deliver programmes, gaining experience through practical projects.The foundation's mental fitness initiatives include resources created by young people and alumni, with guidance from its clinical supervisor and Mental Health Advisory Committee. This arrangement gives students opportunities to contribute to projects that can help others.The #NotAloneChallenge was launched by Jewel and the foundation to raise awareness of mental health challenges and make free behavioural health resources available, particularly in underserved communities.The resources cover several aspects of wellbeing, including managing anxiety, building connections, writing about emotions, practising mindfulness and finding support. The platform also provides material for families, teenagers and communities with specific mental health needs.Leadership and college scholarships remain central to its workMental health support is one part of the foundation's broader programme, which also focuses on helping young people build confidence and prepare for their futures.According to the Inspiring Children Foundation, 95% of students in its leadership programme have earned college scholarships for academics and athletics, including tennis. The organisation says students have received offers from some of the leading colleges in the United States.The programme combines leadership development with mentoring and opportunities to take responsibility for practical projects.A wider effort to make young people feel supportedThe foundation's work also includes community activities that encourage young people to support one another. Its online mental health community, Inspire House, was created by foundation youth during the pandemic and has continued to offer conversations, fitness activities, meditation, music and leadership discussions.The foundation also maintains mentoring relationships between current participants, alumni, staff and supporters. These connections can continue beyond a student's formal participation, with older alumni remaining involved in mentoring younger generations.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Who is Navneet Alag? Meet husband of newly elected Indian-American congresswoman Pia Dandiya
articles.summary: 39-year-old Pia Dandiya is one of the Indian-Americans to have left a mark in the ballot box in the midterms.
articles.body: 39-year-old Pia Dandiya is one of the Indian-Americans to have left a mark in the ballot box in the midterms. The Democratic leader won an election to the US House of Representatives from Florida. A first-time candidate belonging to a family of doctors, Pia may appear to be a chance politician as she has been a teacher and a principal, but she has wanted to be in politics since she was 13. Becoming a Congresswoman at her first election is not a dream come true yet -- when she was a child, she dreamed to be the US president one day.Pia lives in Palm Beach Gardens, Florida, with her husband Navneet Alag and their son, Sahib.Alag, a bioech investor, has maintained a relatively low public profile throughout the campaign. His Linkedin profile indicates that he studied in both India and the US. He has publicly expressed support for Dandiya's political career. In a LinkedIn post in June 2025, when she announced her candidacy for the US House of Representatives, Alag described his reaction as a "proud husband moment"."Pia's commitment to service is something that I have admired about her from the start. Can't wait to see what the future holds!" he wrote. The post was published alongside Dandiya's announcement that she was entering the race for Florida's 21st Congressional District. She subsequently shifted her campaign to the 22nd District following changes to Florida's congressional map.Dandiya was born and raised in Palm Beach County, Florida, to parents who moved to the United States from Jaipur, Rajasthan, in the 1980s.She studied government at Harvard University and earned a master's degree in education from Boston University. She began her career as a teacher with Teach For America and later became the founding principal of Democracy Prep Endurance High School in Harlem, New York.She also served as a White House Fellow in 2020, working with the Domestic Policy Council and the US Department of Education. Later, she worked on public-sector initiatives at Apple.Dandiya has said that her son and her former students were among the reasons she decided to run for Congress.Her victory in Florida's 22nd Congressional District made her the second Indian-American woman elected to the US House of Representatives, after Pramila Jayapal.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2018, Cristiano Ronaldo bought Lisbon’s record-breaking $7 million apartment, before turning a former Madeira nightclub into an $8 million seven-storey home in 2019
articles.summary: Cristiano Ronaldo’s property portfolio stretches across several countries, from luxury residences in Spain and Italy to homes in England and Saudi Arabia.
articles.body: Cristiano Ronaldo’s property portfolio stretches across several countries, from luxury residences in Spain and Italy to homes in England and Saudi Arabia. But two properties in Portugal offer a closer look at his connection to his home country. In Lisbon, the footballer made headlines in 2018 after purchasing an apartment that set a record for the highest price ever paid for a property in the Portuguese capital. As reported by Architectural Digest, a year later, he acquired a very different kind of residence in Madeira, the island where he grew up. The seven-storey building, created from a former warehouse and nightclub, is now reportedly home to his mother and brother.The Lisbon property that became Ronaldo’s most expensive Portuguese apartmentRonaldo's purchase in Lisbon in 2018 attracted attention beyond the football world. The apartment reportedly cost around $7 million, making it the most expensive apartment ever sold in the Portuguese capital at the time.Situated in one of the city's desirable residential areas, the property is not far from another apartment he had acquired in Lisbon three years earlier. The later purchase, however, came with a considerably higher price tag and an extensive collection of luxury facilities.The three-bedroom residence was designed around open spaces and large glass surfaces, allowing natural light to enter much of the interior. Hardwood flooring runs through the property, while a long terrace with a glass balustrade provides views across Lisbon and its surrounding gardens.There is also a considerable amount of space dedicated to leisure and fitness. The apartment includes a private gym, spa facilities and an indoor swimming pool, alongside another pool on the rooftop. The purchase came during Ronaldo's time at Juventus, following his departure from Real Madrid in 2018.How Ronaldo transformed a former warehouse into a luxury Madeira homeA year after the Lisbon purchase, Ronaldo added another property to his Portuguese portfolio, this time in Funchal, the capital of Madeira.The building was previously used as a warehouse and nightclub before being transformed into a private seven-storey home. Ronaldo reportedly spent around $8 million on the conversion, turning the former commercial property near Funchal's port into a modern residence.The building has four floors above ground, with additional levels forming part of its overall structure. Its position near the waterfront gives it views across the Atlantic, while the rooftop includes a swimming pool overlooking the surrounding area.The location also has a personal connection for Ronaldo. Madeira is where he was born and spent his early years before moving to mainland Portugal to pursue his football career.Ronaldo's mother and brother reportedly live there full-timeOne detail that distinguishes the Funchal property from several of Ronaldo's other homes is who reportedly lives there. His mother, Maria Dolores dos Santos Aveiro, and his brother are said to occupy the building full-time. While Ronaldo's professional commitments have taken him between different countries, the Madeira residence provides a home for members of his immediate family in the place where he grew up.Ronaldo's family has remained a familiar part of his public life over the years. His mother has frequently appeared alongside him at important football occasions, while his siblings have also maintained connections to Madeira.The seven-storey property therefore stands apart from the more conventional luxury apartments and villas associated with the footballer's name. Its previous use as a warehouse and nightclub makes its transformation particularly distinctive within his collection of residences.Portugal remains an important part of Ronaldo's property portfolioRonaldo's investments in Lisbon and Madeira form part of a much wider collection of properties accumulated during his career. His first major property purchase in England came after his move to Manchester United. In 2007, he bought a five-bedroom house in Alderley Edge, near Manchester, reportedly for around $7.1 million. The property included an indoor swimming pool, gym, steam room and private cinema. He eventually sold it in 2019, reportedly at a loss.During his Real Madrid years, he also acquired properties in La Finca, an exclusive neighbourhood in the Spanish capital. The two modern residences covered approximately 8,600 square feet and included extensive leisure facilities, among them an indoor pool, sauna, Jacuzzi and cryotherapy chamber.His move to Italy in 2018 brought another residential purchase. In Turin, Ronaldo and his family lived in a secluded compound consisting of two modern villas, with large windows, a garden, swimming pool, spa and gym. He also owned a property in Marbella, Spain, and an apartment in New York's Trump Tower, which he purchased in 2015 for around $18 million. The Manhattan apartment was eventually sold in 2022 for approximately $7.18 million, after spending several years on the market.Disclaimer: This article is based on information publicly available. articles.summary: Speculations that President Donald Trump would fire Susie Wiles have been doing the rounds long before the embarrassing midterm loss that the Republicans
articles.body: Speculations that President Donald Trump would fire Susie Wiles have been doing the rounds long before the embarrassing midterm loss that the Republicans suffered. Politico reported that Trump was ringing up his allies to explore some options to replace Wiles. The 2,676-word statement, published on X on November 4, 2026, included his views on several sensitive subjects. G2 CEO Alban Dechelotte announced the decision on November 5, saying some of Perkz's comments did not match the organization's values. Meanwhile, popular esports host Sjokz has also spoken about the situation and her own mental health.G2 Esports Ends Its Relationship With Luka Perkz After His Comments on Abortion and Other IssuesPerkz's post covered several parts of his personal life, including his father's death, his marriage and his return to G2. He explained that he wanted to address claims about him that he believed were false. However, his comments about abortion became the main point of discussion.The Croatian coach revealed that he had become closer to God in recent years and now considered himself a practising Catholic. While explaining his religious beliefs, he shared his strong opposition to abortion."The only thing that is unshakeable for me [...] is abortion; I cannot comprehend how people do not understand that it is murder, as life is created at conception," Perkz wrote.His post also addressed his past connection with Andrew and Tristan Tate. Perkz denied supporting the brothers and said liking their memes in 2022 had been a mistake."I don't like, support, or stand with the Tates. I hate most of the things they say," he explained.He also defended his relationship with former G2 CEO Carlos "ocelote" Rodríguez, who faced criticism over his association with the Tate brothers. He explained that the organization respects people from different backgrounds and cultures. However, some of Perkz's views did not match its position."We acknowledge that this statement hurt many of our fans, and we want to apologize for it," Dechelotte said.He then confirmed that G2 had decided to terminate its relationship with the coach. The organization also said it would now focus on rebuilding its staff and roster for the next season.Perkz later shared a Bible verse on X. However, by November 6, his account had been deactivated, although screenshots of his original post continued to circulate.Sjokz Speaks About Perkz's Controversial Comments and Her Mental HealthThe controversy also drew a response from Eefje "Sjokz" Depoortere, one of the best-known hosts in the League of Legends community.The Belgian presenter spoke about where she stands on the issues being discussed in the community. However, she also admitted that constantly speaking up for the things she believes in has become difficult for her."Currently, in our community, you should know where I stand, you know where I stand," Sjokz said.She then explained that she does not always have the mental strength to keep fighting for the causes that matter to her."At this point in time my mental health is hanging on by the smallest of threads," she added.Sjokz also pointed out that her work requires her to cover important events and remain active in the esports community.
